270.bp: A recommender has to choose a few useful items from a much larger pile. In an online shop, video feed, or content platform, the real unit a person cares about is the item: this shirt, this movie, this product variant, this next thing to inspect. The paper asks what happens when a language model handles that item by first breaking its description into small word pieces, called tokens, and then lets every piece look at other pieces while forming a recommendation. That helps the model read item text, such as name, color, and size, but it can blur a basic boundary: which words belong together as one item, and which words indicate relations between different items. The practical need is therefore not just better text understanding. It is to make a language-model recommender respect the item as the decision object, because the final action is to rank items for users, not to rank isolated words.
270.wh: The hard part is that recommendation needs two kinds of evidence at once. First, the system must understand what a single item is. The words inside one item description may describe its name, color, size, or other content. Second, the system must learn how items relate across user behavior: items bought, clicked, watched, or preferred together can carry collaborative evidence. A standard attention layer, meaning a learned weighting rule that decides which small text pieces should influence one another, usually works at the level of tokens. If all token relations are mixed together, the model may treat a word inside one item description and a word inside another item description as just another pair of pieces. That is too flat for recommendation. The model may learn token-level patterns while missing the item-level relation that actually matters: users choose among whole items, and collaborative preference is a relation between items, not merely between their words.
270.naive: A smart beginner would take each item, write it as a sequence of tokens, place user history and candidate items into a language model, and let the model's ordinary attention layers discover the useful relations. This is tempting because language models are built to process sequences, and item titles or attributes look like text. The failure is boundary loss. The model can spend its effort connecting token to token without being told whether two tokens are part of the same item or part of different items. That means product description evidence and collaborative item evidence can be tangled. The recommender may know that words co-occur, yet still fail to represent that one complete item tends to be chosen with another complete item.
270.ap: The paper's central move is to split the model's focusing step according to the item boundary. It categorizes token relations into two types. Intra-item relations are relations among tokens inside the same item; these are meant to capture the item's content semantics, such as how name, color, and size fit together into a coherent product description. Inter-item relations are relations across items; these are meant to capture collaborative relations, the behavioral pattern that some items belong near one another in recommendation because of user choices. The proposed item-aware attention mechanism builds two complementary layers around that split. One layer restricts attention to tokens within the same item. The other attends only to token relations across items. Stacking these layers makes the recommender read each item as an item first, then compare items as items, instead of letting all word pieces compete in one undifferentiated pool.
270.mech: The mechanism begins with the normal input to an LLM-driven recommender: items are represented as token sequences. The abstract does not give the full implementation beyond this point, but it does state the key routing rule. The system keeps track of which tokens belong to which item. In the intra-item attention layer, a token is allowed to draw information only from tokens inside the same item boundary. If an item description contains a name, color, and size, those pieces can influence one another so the model forms a more coherent view of that item. This layer is about item content, not user co-choice. Next, the inter-item attention layer changes the allowed comparison. It attends exclusively to token relations across items. That means evidence can move between item descriptions only when the relation crosses item boundaries, which is where collaborative recommendation information is supposed to live. The two layers are stacked, so the output of one focusing operation feeds the next. What comes out is still a representation used for recommendation and ranking, but its internal path has separated two jobs: understand the parts of each item, then capture relations among items. The paper calls this item-aware attention because the weighting rule is no longer blind to item membership.
270.math: The main mathematical idea is weighted influence with a mask, where a mask is a rule that says which comparisons are allowed and which are blocked. Ordinary attention gives each part of an input a learned weight saying how much it should influence another part. In everyday terms, it is a way of deciding who gets heard when many small pieces of evidence are speaking at once. This paper changes the comparison set before the weights are used. For intra-item attention, the allowed set contains only tokens from the same item, so the weighted average summarizes content within a boundary. For inter-item attention, the allowed set contains relations across item boundaries, so the weighted evidence is aimed at collaborative item relations. Ranking is the second mathematical idea: after the model builds useful item information, candidates must still be scored and ordered for recommendation. The tradeoff is focus versus blindness. Restricting comparisons can remove confusing token-level noise, but it can also block a relation if the boundary rule is too rigid. The math fits because the practical error comes from uncontrolled mixing; the remedy is controlled comparison.
270.dots: This paper sits in the recommender-systems family described in the repo: systems must choose a small useful set from a huge, changing pile, using partial evidence from text and behavior. It connects directly to ranking, because the final recommender still has to score item usefulness and sort candidates. It also connects to similarity and collaborative filtering, because inter-item relations are a way of saying that items can be near one another when users treat them as related, not only when their descriptions share words. The attention concept file frames this as selective influence: some pieces of evidence should speak loudly and others should stay quiet. This paper applies that idea to item boundaries. Neighboring LLM recommendation papers in the repo handle fairness, preference editing, graph alignment, multiple language models, and deployment cost. This one targets a more basic representation problem: before those higher-level concerns, the model must know what counts as the item being recommended.
270.ww: The approach should help when the naive model's mistake is mixing two different meanings of relation. Inside an item, relation means description coherence: the name, color, size, and other words jointly define what the item is. Across items, relation means recommendation evidence: one item may be useful because it appears with, substitutes for, or complements another in user behavior. A single token-centric focusing rule can blur those meanings because it sees a broad table of token-to-token interactions. The item-aware design improves the situation by making the path of information match the structure of the task. First, each item can become internally coherent without being immediately pulled apart by other item descriptions. Then cross-item evidence can be modeled as cross-item evidence rather than accidental word contact. This is not magic; it works only if the item boundaries in the input are meaningful and if collaborative relations can be learned from the available item-level patterns. But when those conditions hold, the model's comparisons are better aligned with the actual recommendation decision.
270.po: The payoff is a language-model recommender that treats items as the fundamental recommendation unit while still using token-level text processing. The abstract says IAM explicitly separates intra-item content semantics from inter-item collaborative relations through two complementary attention layers. That buys a cleaner modeling path: understand what each item says about itself, then learn how items relate to other items for recommendation. The repo's analysis summarizes the contribution as enhanced LLM recommendation through hierarchical item-level collaborative modeling. Because the abstract is truncated, the available evidence does not support specific claims about datasets, metric gains, or deployment speed.
270.limits: The method assumes that item boundaries are available and useful. If the input formatting does not clearly say which tokens belong to which item, the layer restrictions may enforce the wrong structure. It also assumes that intra-item text and inter-item collaborative relations are separable enough to benefit from different focusing layers; some recommendation clues may mix content and behavior in ways this split oversimplifies. The abstract does not show the full architecture, training objective, experiments, or failure cases because the repository text is truncated. It therefore supports the mechanism-level claim, but not broad claims about general performance, fairness, cold-start behavior, cost, or reliability across domains.

271.bp: The real-world job is making a film, show, or online video understandable in another language without flattening the people speaking in it. Subtitles are not ordinary paragraphs. They arrive in short bursts, tied to faces, voices, timing, character relationships, recurring names, and emotional delivery. A viewer needs to know not only what a sentence means, but who said it, what earlier lines it depends on, and whether the line is formal, joking, angry, tender, or dramatic. This paper serves entertainment localization: the work of carrying visual media across languages for audiences who still need the story to feel coherent. The abstract says this specific setting, interlingual subtitling, has not yet been deeply explored inside machine translation. Hermes is presented as an automated subtitling system built around the fact that subtitle translation needs speaker tracking, consistent terminology, and expressive wording, not just sentence-level word replacement.
271.wh: The hard part is that subtitles hide important context inside pieces that look too small to translate safely on their own. A single subtitle line may contain a pronoun such as he, she, they, or you, but the correct translation can depend on the speaker, the addressee, gender, social relation, or earlier scene. A named object, place, title, or technical phrase may appear many times, and inconsistent translation can make the plot feel broken. Expressiveness is harder still because a literal sentence can be correct in dictionary meaning and still sound wrong for the scene. Large language models have improved general translation, but the abstract says subtitle text keeps causing trouble in semantic coherence, pronoun and terminology translation, and expressive translation. These difficulties are connected: if the system loses track of who is speaking, it may choose the wrong pronoun; if it loses the term inventory, later lines stop matching earlier ones; if it ignores delivery, the translation becomes emotionally thin.
271.naive: A smart beginner would take each subtitle line, send it to a strong general translator, and paste the translated line back into the video. That is attractive because subtitles already look like separate text snippets. It fails because each snippet is only a visible piece of a larger scene. The translator may not know which character speaks, so pronouns and forms of address can drift. It may translate an important term one way in one scene and another way later. It may preserve basic meaning but lose the attitude of the original line. Another beginner fix is to translate a larger block of subtitles at once, but that still does not explicitly assign speakers, identify terms that need stable handling, or ask for expressive adjustment tied to the subtitle setting.
271.ap: The paper's core idea is to treat interlingual subtitling as several coupled decisions instead of one generic translation request. Hermes is described as a large-language-model-based automated subtitling system with three modules. Speaker Diarization decides which subtitle segments belong to which speaker, giving the translation process a stable sense of who is talking. Terminology Identification finds words or phrases that need careful, consistent handling, such as names, recurring concepts, or domain-specific expressions. Expressiveness Enhancement then works on the translated subtitle so it carries more than literal meaning: it should sound contextually coherent and better matched to the force of the original line. The central mechanical move is decomposition. Instead of hoping one translation pass silently solves every hidden dependency, Hermes names the three pressure points and gives each a place in the pipeline.
271.mech: The input is visual media with subtitle text that must be translated into a target language. Hermes first has to make the subtitle stream more structured. The Speaker Diarization module groups or labels subtitle segments by speaker, turning a loose list of lines into a sequence where each line has a likely voice behind it. That matters because speaker identity anchors pronouns, turn-taking, and continuity across nearby lines. The Terminology Identification module then scans for expressions whose translation should not be left to chance each time they appear. It marks terms that need stable treatment so the system can avoid translating the same story object, role, or technical phrase in conflicting ways. With those two kinds of context available, the translation step can use a large language model, a text model trained to predict and produce language, with more guidance than a plain sentence-by-sentence call. The Expressiveness Enhancement module then revises or steers the output toward wording that better preserves tone and naturalness in the target language. The system therefore transforms raw subtitle lines into speaker-aware, term-aware, expressive target-language subtitles. The output is not only translated text, but a subtitle track intended to remain coherent across scenes and emotionally closer to the original media.
271.math: The main mathematical ideas are matching, sequence context, controlled rewriting, and scoring choices under constraints. Speaker diarization is a matching problem: the system observes pieces of a media stream and decides which pieces should be assigned to the same speaker identity. In everyday terms, it asks which lines belong together because they come from the same person, even when the text alone may be short or ambiguous. Terminology identification is a selection problem: among many words, it chooses the ones whose unstable translation would cause later confusion. That is a kind of importance scoring, where repeated or meaning-bearing expressions receive special attention. Translation itself is probabilistic generation: the language model chooses a target sentence by estimating which word sequence is plausible given the source text and context. Expressiveness enhancement is constrained rewriting. The rewrite should move the subtitle toward natural tone while preserving the underlying meaning and fitting the subtitle role. The tradeoff is meaning faithfulness versus expressive freedom. Too little freedom gives stiff literal subtitles; too much freedom risks changing the story. Hermes fits the problem because subtitling naturally asks for assignment, selection, and careful rewriting, not just one undifferentiated text conversion.
271.dots: This paper connects to several recurring conference ideas even though its surface topic is media translation. It is part of language-model work because it uses a large text model as a translation engine, but it also shows why broad language ability is not enough when the application has structure outside the sentence. It connects to multimodal work because subtitle meaning is tied to visual media and speakers, not just written text. It connects to sequence reasoning because coherence depends on what came before and who has been speaking over time. It also relates to information extraction: terminology identification pulls out the pieces of text that deserve special control. Compared with retrieval or recommendation papers that rank candidates from a huge pile, Hermes ranks and chooses among possible translations under scene-level constraints. The shared deeper issue is context: a system must decide which surrounding evidence should shape the current output.
271.ww: Hermes should improve over the naive approach because it reduces the number of hidden decisions left for a general translator to guess. When speaker identity is explicit, the model has better evidence for pronouns, social phrasing, and continuity of dialogue. Even if the abstract does not spell out the exact diarization features, the principle is clear: a line spoken by one character carries different translation obligations than the same words spoken by another. When terminology is identified, the system can treat repeated important phrases as stable objects rather than independent accidents. That directly attacks one source of viewer confusion: the same thing being named differently across scenes. Expressiveness enhancement helps because subtitles are performed language. The target wording must be readable, natural, and emotionally appropriate, while still carrying the source meaning. Decomposing the pipeline works because each module attacks a distinct failure mode, and the later translation has more structured context than a plain line-by-line prompt. The reported experiments support this direction by showing strong diarization and contextually coherent, expressive translations.
271.po: The payoff is an automated subtitling system that addresses the specific pains of entertainment localization rather than treating video subtitles as ordinary machine-translation input. According to the abstract, Hermes achieves state-of-the-art speaker diarization performance and produces translations that are expressive and contextually coherent. In practical terms, that means a localization workflow could get subtitles that better preserve who is speaking, keep important terms consistent, and carry more of the original tone. The broader research payoff is that interlingual subtitling becomes a named machine-translation problem with modules and evaluation targets instead of an informal extension of generic translation.
271.limits: The abstract supports the existence and reported performance of Hermes, but it does not prove every part will generalize to all languages, genres, subtitle styles, or production settings. Speaker diarization must be accurate enough; wrong speaker labels could make pronoun and tone choices worse. Terminology identification must find the terms that matter without over-controlling ordinary words. Expressiveness enhancement assumes the model can change style while preserving meaning, which is a delicate balance. The abstract mentions experiments and state-of-the-art diarization, but does not provide the datasets, language pairs, human evaluation details, latency, cost, or failure cases here. It also does not show how the system handles cultural adaptation, strict subtitle length limits, or scenes where visual context contradicts text.

272.bp: A real-time recommendation system has to make a hard promise: when a person searches or browses creative content, it must sort many possible items quickly, and the order should feel reasonable enough to trust. Large language and vision-language models can inspect text and images together and often make richer semantic judgments, such as whether a piece of content fits a query beyond surface word overlap. The problem is that these large teachers are too heavy for the moment when a search page or recommendation feed must be served. This paper asks whether their useful ranking behavior can be carried by a much smaller text-only ranker. TCR serves that need: it tries to keep the teacher models' richer multimodal reasoning while removing the image-processing and massive-model cost that would block production use. The practical object is not a chatbot answer, but an ordered list of content where trust, calibration, transparency, and delay all matter.
272.wh: The difficulty comes from a three-way squeeze. First, creative content and interactive search often need semantic judgment: the system must understand what a query is asking for and which content actually fits, even when wording, style, and visual meaning do not line up exactly. Second, the strongest models for that judgment are large language and vision-language models, which means systems that read language and images together at high computational cost. They can reason well, but they are impractical when millions of query-content decisions must be made with production-grade delay. Third, a recommender is judged not only by whether the top item is relevant, but by whether its scores are calibrated, meaning the score strength matches real confidence, and whether users can perceive the system as trustworthy. A small ranker may be fast but shallow; a large teacher may be smart but slow. The hard part is preserving the right ordering behavior under a severe size and speed budget.
272.naive: A smart beginner would either run the best multimodal large model directly at ranking time or discard it and train a small text ranker from ordinary labels. The first option fails because every query-content pair would require expensive reasoning, making real-time recommendation and search too slow and costly. The second option fails in the opposite direction: the small model sees only the final labels and may miss the soft differences the teacher noticed, such as two relevant items where one is a better fit. A third simple option is to copy one teacher exactly. That can inherit one model's blind spots and miscalibration. TCR exists because the useful target is not just a label; it is a ranking judgment with graded confidence gathered from multiple stronger teachers.
272.ap: The core idea is to turn heavy multimodal reasoning into training signal for a compact text-only ranker. TCR uses multiple vision-language large models as teachers. Instead of asking the deployed system to look at images with those teachers every time, the teachers first produce soft labels for query-content pairs. A soft label is not merely right or wrong; it carries a degree of preference or confidence, which teaches the smaller model about near misses and strong matches. The paper then fuses the teachers' signals, so the student is not tied to one teacher's peculiar judgments. The student is a DeBERTa-based cross-attention ranker: it reads the query and content text together so each side can influence the interpretation of the other. LoRA fine-tuning changes only a small set of added parameters, making adaptation cheaper. The result is meant to rank like the teachers while serving like a small text model.
272.mech: The mechanism starts with real-world query-content pairs, 4.4 million of them according to the abstract. For each pair, the system needs a judgment about how the content should be ordered for that query. The heavy teacher stage uses several vision-language large language models to reason over the richer evidence available during training. Their outputs are converted into soft labels, which means the training target keeps graded preference information instead of flattening everything into a single yes-or-no answer. Those teacher signals are then fused across teachers. In plain terms, the student receives a blended lesson: if several strong teachers agree that one pair is highly relevant, that signal is strong; if their views differ, the target can reflect weaker or more uncertain evidence. Next, the DeBERTa-based student receives text for the query and text for the content. Cross-attention, a comparison operation where words from the query and words from the content can directly influence one another, lets the model judge fit pair by pair rather than encoding each side in isolation. LoRA fine-tuning adapts the ranker by learning small add-on weight changes instead of rewriting the whole model. At serving time, the output is a ranking score for each candidate pair, used to re-order content quickly without running the multimodal teachers.
272.math: The mathematical ideas are ranking, distillation, calibration, attention, and parameter-efficient adaptation. Ranking turns many candidate content items into an order by giving each query-content pair a score. The score is useful only because it decides which item should stand above another under limited user attention. Distillation means training a smaller student to imitate useful behavior from larger teachers. Here the copied behavior is not just a final class label; it is a softer pattern of preferences across candidate pairs. Multi-teacher fusion is an averaging or combining problem: several imperfect judges produce signals, and the training target tries to keep their shared information while reducing dependence on any one judge. Calibration means matching score strength to actual trustworthiness, so a high score should mean the model has stronger evidence, not merely louder confidence. Cross-attention is a weighted comparison: each part of the query can ask which parts of the content matter for this decision, and vice versa. LoRA is low-rank adaptation, meaning a compact set of added weight changes that restricts how much of the model must be updated. The tradeoff is compression versus detail: TCR must preserve enough teacher reasoning to rank well while discarding the heavy visual machinery that made the teachers expensive.
272.dots: This paper connects directly to the repo's recommender-systems family, where many papers face the same pressure of choosing a small useful set from a huge pile under delay and uncertainty. It also sits inside multimodal vision-language work, but with a deployment twist: instead of using image-and-language reasoning at serving time, it compresses that reasoning into a text-only ranker. The ranking concept is central because the real decision is comparative, not absolute; TCR succeeds if better content reliably rises above weaker content near the top of the list. It also touches the efficiency and scalability family because the abstract reports a 98.5 percent parameter reduction and production-grade latency, making cost part of the scientific claim rather than an afterthought. Finally, the trust theme appears through calibration and transparency. The paper is about a familiar 2026 pattern: use large models to create richer supervision, then deploy a smaller model that can survive real traffic.
272.ww: TCR should work better than the naive small ranker because it learns from the teachers' ordering behavior rather than from a thin target alone. A hard label might say two items are both relevant, but a teacher can imply that one is a cleaner semantic match, one is borderline, or one is relevant only under a weaker interpretation of the query. Those graded differences are exactly what ranking needs near the top of the list. Using multiple teachers can also smooth out single-teacher quirks: if one vision-language model overvalues a visual clue while another does not, fusion can reduce the chance that the student copies that mistake completely. Cross-attention helps because query meaning and content meaning are not independent; the same content phrase may matter for one query and be irrelevant for another. LoRA helps on the cost side by adapting the model without carrying the full training burden of a huge system. The method works only if the text representation still contains enough traces of the multimodal reasoning the teachers used.
272.po: The payoff is a recommender or search reranker that keeps much of the semantic judgment of heavier vision-language teachers while fitting real-time production constraints. The abstract claims a 98.5 percent parameter reduction, production-grade latency, and near-teacher ranking quality on 4.4 million real-world query-content pairs. That matters because it changes multimodal reasoning from an offline luxury into a deployable ranking signal for creative content and interactive search. The system also aims to make recommendation more trust-aware by aligning calibration and transparency with user-perceived trust, so the score is not treated as a private black box detached from user confidence.
272.limits: The abstract does not prove that text alone can preserve every visual cue the teachers used. If an item's key relevance comes from an image detail absent from its text, the student may copy only an approximation. The method also depends on teacher quality: fused soft labels are useful only if the teachers' judgments are mostly reliable and their errors are not shared. Calibration and transparency are named as trust goals, but the abstract does not describe the human study or interface evidence needed to prove user-perceived trust broadly. The reported 4.4 million pairs are real-world data, but the claim may depend on that platform's content, queries, traffic patterns, and latency requirements.

273.bp: Imagine a warehouse manager searching inventory not just by description but by rules—"show me red shoes available today that arrived last week." Real data has both unstructured pieces (what something looks like) and structured pieces (when it arrived, how many remain). Combining both kinds of questions in a single search is called a hybrid query, and it's essential everywhere: e-commerce, medical records, news archives. But doing it fast and accurately at scale is surprisingly hard.
273.wh: Existing search systems excel at either keywords or numerical/time filters, but not both at once. When you try to do both, you face a trap: use loose filtering to avoid missing results, and you search through mountains of irrelevant data (slow). Use strict filtering, and you accidentally exclude items that should match (wrong answers). Getting speed *and* correctness together requires a fundamentally different approach to how data is organized.
273.ap: The authors propose organizing data into subgroups based on time or other attributes—like sorting a library by century first, then by topic within each century. Within each subgroup, they build a graph index that can handle flexible search patterns. When you pose a hybrid query, the system first narrows down to the relevant subgroups (fast, because there are few), then searches within those subgroups using the graph (precise, because you're not searching everything). Finally, they add a logical query layer that can combine results in complex ways.
273.ww: This works because it respects a fundamental truth: time and other properties create natural boundaries in data. A shoe that arrived last week and one that arrived last year truly are different in important ways, so organizing around those boundaries isn't losing information—it's reflecting reality. The graph index within each boundary can focus on semantic matching without worrying about time shifts. Together, these layers let you get the best of both worlds: you avoid the irrelevant masses without accidentally filtering away valid answers.
273.po: Testing on nine benchmark datasets, the method outperforms seven existing systems on both speed and accuracy. It handles hybrid queries—combining unstructured similarity with structured constraints—without the slowness or accuracy loss of current methods, making it practical for web-scale applications where both types of search are essential.

274.bp: When a search engine shows you ads, it's a silent auction: advertisers bid to appear in prime positions. That auction model worked for decades with text ads in fixed slots. Now imagine an AI generates an article for you, and an advertiser wants to embed a product mention mid-paragraph—not in a side slot. The old auction rules break because the new context is fluid: the effectiveness of an ad now depends entirely on where and how it's woven into the text. This paper asks: how should we charge advertisers when context itself is being generated?
274.wh: Classic position auctions assume that slots are independent—if ad A is in position 2 and ad B is in position 3, moving B doesn't change how many people see A. But when ads are embedded in AI-generated prose, they're not independent anymore. A product mentioned early in an article might *substitute* for one mentioned later ("I already know what brand to buy"), creating complex dependencies that the old math doesn't handle.
274.ap: The authors formalize a model where an AI system can place sponsored content at any point in generated text, and they study two user behavior models. In the multinomial model, a user's choice is balanced across all positions (like scrolling through independent options). In the cascade model, users read top-to-bottom and stop once satisfied (like clicking through search results)—so position matters hugely, and substitution effects are strong. For each model, they derive what the optimal auction mechanism should be.
274.ww: For the multinomial model, positions are independent enough that classical auction theory applies—you can use standard tricks to ensure prices are fair and total value is maximized. For the cascade model, position order creates strong substitution: the paper shows you can't achieve perfect optimality (the math says it's hard), but you *can* find approximately optimal mechanisms by carefully considering how users' decisions flow down the page.
274.po: The paper provides concrete auction mechanisms for both behaviors, with proofs about their optimality guarantees. This matters because it gives platforms a mathematical foundation for pricing ads in AI-generated content: they can now charge fairly for position while accounting for the fact that earlier positions suppress click-through on later ones. Without this, advertisers would either overpay or underpay, and platforms would leave revenue on the table.

275.bp: The web is "free" because advertising pays for it—but that freedom comes with a cost often invisible to users: energy. Every ad displayed, tracked, and measured burns electricity on your device. As climate concerns grow and energy costs rise, the hidden environmental toll of advertising deserves scrutiny. This paper measures something nobody usually asks: how much battery does an ad actually drain from your phone or laptop over a year?
275.wh: Energy consumption on a user's device is hard to measure accurately because CPUs vary, websites vary, and user behavior varies wildly. You can't just run ads once in a lab and extrapolate—real users sleep their devices, switch tabs, have different hardware. Additionally, ads come bundled with tracking systems (cookies, analytics, real-time bidding auctions) that each add their own compute overhead, and it's unclear which component is responsible for the drain.
275.ap: The authors measure energy consumption directly across nearly 725,000 real website visits on real devices (phones, tablets, laptops), monitoring actual CPU usage while ads load and track. They measure three scenarios: visiting sites with cookie consent enabled, sites with ads blocked, and sites relying on real-time bidding (rapid auctions for each ad slot). They use robust methodology to model realistic user behavior—not every visit keeps a tab active for hours, for instance.
275.ww: By measuring at scale across diverse devices and behaviors, the paper captures real-world inefficiency. The key insight is that ads and tracking aren't just downloading data—they're running algorithms (bidding, profiling, ranking) on your device. Energy draws from processing, not just bandwidth. Cookie consent banners make sites run *more* tracking code (not less), and real-time bidding triggers constant auctions, both burning compute.
275.po: The results are concrete: cookie banners increase energy consumption by 2.57% on average, and real-time bidding increases it by 34% on average. Over a year, for a typical user, that's measurable impact. The paper quantifies the environmental cost of the ad ecosystem that nobody usually discusses, giving advocates and policymakers ammunition for conversations about web sustainability and fairness to users.

276.bp: Recommendation systems are shifting from a single recommender algorithm making all decisions to multiple AI agents negotiating with each other—one for discovering products, another for fulfilling orders, another for conversing with you. These agents can plan together, argue about priorities, and adapt in real time. The challenge is that when multiple agents act autonomously, old evaluation metrics (did you click? did you buy?) no longer capture what matters: Can we trust the system? Do recommendations stay fair to everyone? Do multiple agents' goals align or conflict?
276.wh: Classic recommendation metrics measure short-term user engagement or immediate sales. But when agents coordinate over longer timescales, new problems emerge: one agent's action may have delayed effects that another agent can't see; if agents disagree, one may override the other's decision, creating unpredictability; fairness becomes multi-dimensional (fair to users, sellers, and the platform itself). Worse, there's no standard way to *evaluate* coordination quality, trustworthiness, or alignment across populations.
276.ap: The authors organize a workshop bringing together researchers in recommender systems, multi-agent learning, and mechanism design. They seek contributions on three fronts: agent architectures (how to build agents that talk to each other), coordination mechanisms (rules for how agents negotiate), and evaluation frameworks (metrics that capture coordination quality, not just clicks). The implicit goal is to establish shared principles and benchmarks.
276.ww: Multi-agent systems are fundamentally harder to reason about because you have to reason about *interactions*—not just individual agent decisions but how they influence each other. By bringing together the subcommunities (recommendation specialists, agents researchers, mechanism designers), the workshop aims to cross-pollinate ideas: mechanism design has formal tools for coordination, agents research has architectures for autonomy, and recommender systems has real-world deployment experience.
276.po: The workshop output is an emerging set of principles for building trustworthy multi-agent recommendation systems, including evaluation frameworks that measure coordination quality alongside traditional metrics. The paper catalyzes research that bridges a gap: how to move recommendation systems from single algorithms to coordinative agent teams without sacrificing interpretability, robustness, or fairness.

277.bp: When you search for similar documents in a massive library, systems now convert each document to a single high-dimensional vector and find neighbors by geometric distance. This works surprisingly well—until it doesn't. Some recent studies have shown that even the best models fail dramatically on small, focused retrieval tasks with simple queries, suggesting a fundamental limit to this approach. The question is: within those limits, can you still make meaningful improvements?
277.wh: High-dimensional vector search has a mathematical ceiling: a single vector can only encode so much information before it becomes hopelessly compressed. Imagine trying to describe a book using just 100 numbers—you'll lose nuance no matter how clever you are. Additionally, when you stuff everything into high dimensions, the "curse of dimensionality" kicks in: the notion of distance itself breaks down, and nearby vectors may not actually be semantically similar.
277.ap: The authors test whether simple dimensionality reduction—taking the 100 numbers and projecting them to, say, 50 dimensions—helps. They also experiment with meta-embedding, a technique that combines multiple vector representations from the same document into a better single vector. The idea is to see whether the theoretical ceiling is the *only* problem or whether over-parameterization (using too many dimensions) compounds the difficulty.
277.ww: Dimensionality reduction helps because it forces the model to retain only the *essential* semantic distinctions—noise and overfitting get pruned away. Meta-embedding works because different representations of the same document sometimes capture different aspects (one model sees "red car" through color, another through vehicle type), and combining them creates a richer, less-compressed summary.
277.po: The paper shows that within the theoretical limits of single-vector retrieval, simple techniques like dimensionality reduction improve performance by 7%, and meta-embedding adds another 2%. While this doesn't overcome the theoretical ceiling, it meaningfully narrows the gap compared to multi-vector systems. The takeaway: even against fundamental constraints, smart representation choices matter.

278.bp: Watermarks embedded in AI-generated images are meant to prove you created an image (or prevent unauthorized copying). These watermarks are invisible to the human eye but detectable by software. As watermarking has grown smarter—binding the watermark to the image's *meaning*, not just its pixels—experts believed they'd finally solved the problem. But this paper shows that large language models can think their way around even these semantic watermarks, exposing a new vulnerability.
278.wh: Early watermarks lived in noise layers and were easy to strip away by simple image edits. Semantic watermarks tried to fix this by tying the watermark to high-level meaning—if you edit the image, the semantics change and the watermark breaks. But this assumes attackers can only make local edits. Large language models, however, can reason about global image meaning and find edits that change the watermark signal *without* breaking what the image represents.
278.ap: The authors propose an attack called Coherence-Preserving Semantic Injection. An LLM first reasons about the image's semantic space, identifying which aspects of the image's meaning are tied to the watermark. Then the LLM finds edits that change those watermark-relevant aspects while keeping everything else consistent—like rearranging a room's furniture while maintaining "homeyness". The attack uses embedding-space similarity to ensure the edited image still *feels* like the original.
278.ww: The attack works because LLMs can reason about semantics *holistically*. A human might edit a car from red to blue; a watermark-aware system would catch this because color is obviously semantic. But an LLM can realize that changing the car's style subtly—say, from sporty to luxurious—also changes semantic meaning in ways the watermark cares about, while still keeping the image coherent and recognizable.
278.po: The paper demonstrates that LLM-guided semantic attacks consistently defeat current semantic watermarks, revealing that binding watermarks to meaning alone doesn't make them robust. The implication is that watermark designers need to account for adversaries with reasoning capabilities, not just pixel-level manipulation tools—a fundamental shift in how to think about image authentication.

279.bp: Building software today often means a programmer and an AI pair up—the AI suggests code, the programmer reviews it, maybe asks the AI to fix bugs or write tests. The dream is to automate more of this workflow: not just completing lines, but planning what to build, testing thoroughly, handling failures without human intervention, and integrating smoothly into existing development tools. This paper surveys how multiple AI agents can team up to replace the fragmented, single-model-per-task approach with structured, coordinated workflows.
279.wh: Most AI coding tools treat each task independently: code completion, bug fixing, test generation, code review. But real development is sequential and interconnected—you can't test until you've coded, you can't deploy until tests pass, you can't review without knowing the spec. Jumping between disconnected models loses context, and no single model sees the full picture of what's being built.
279.ap: The authors synthesize examples from GitHub Copilot, Mistral Codec, and other systems to show a pattern: specialized agent teams with defined roles (code writer, test engineer, reviewer), a manager that routes tasks based on what's needed, and shared tools (the codebase, version control, CI/CD systems). Agents maintain long-term memory of decisions and mistakes, and can query each other's work to avoid redundant effort.
279.ww: Role specialization means each agent gets expert prompting for its task (code completion is different from test design). Coordination through a manager prevents bottlenecks and ensures agents work in the right order. Shared memory means later agents can learn from earlier agents' experiments—if the first attempt at implementing feature X failed, the test agent won't waste time testing broken code.
279.po: The result is a reproducible, auditable development workflow where agents check each other's work, integrate with real CI/CD pipelines, and close the loop from specification to deployment. The paper provides practical patterns for reliability, security, and cost efficiency, showing that collaborative multi-agent systems can deliver measurable productivity gains and fewer human reviews needed.

280.bp: When a user's interests change over time—maybe you watch comedy for a month, then switch to documentaries—a good recommendation system should notice and adapt quickly. But it also shouldn't forget that you like comedy in general. Getting this balance right while protecting user privacy and not requiring constant retraining is the challenge of continual personalization in real-world systems.
280.wh: Standard recommendation systems are either static (trained once, never updated) or centralized (requiring all user data on one server, a privacy nightmare). Federated learning lets models improve across millions of users without moving their data, but it's slow and doesn't capture rapid shifts in intent. Additionally, distinguishing between a user's long-term taste and their current mood is hard—the system might mistake a one-week binge for a permanent shift.
280.ap: The authors propose ProtoFed-SP, which uses soft prompts (learnable modifications to a frozen model) in a two-layer structure. A fast short-term prompt updates each session to capture session intent (what the user is looking for *right now*). A slow long-term prompt anchors to a small library of prototype users maintained on the server, refreshed using privacy-preserving federated methods. When recommending, the system picks the top matching prototypes and blends their personalized prompts.
280.ww: Two-timescale learning mirrors how humans actually adapt: you have lasting preferences (anchored to prototypes of users like you) and temporary impulses (the fast session prompt). The server-side prototype library prevents forgetting—individual users train locally, but prototypes persist and benefit from all users' data simultaneously. Differential privacy on the federation means the server never sees raw user data.
280.po: Across eight benchmark datasets, ProtoFed-SP improves recommendation quality by 2-5% and reduces catastrophic forgetting. Users benefit from both quick adaptation to session context and stability from long-term memory. The system respects privacy (federated + differential privacy) while delivering personalization that works in real deployments.

281.bp: Recommending the next item a user will interact with requires understanding what each item *is* and how it relates to the user's past. Product databases give you structured metadata (name, price, category), but that's shallow. Large language models can read descriptions and infer deeper meaning. The question is: how do you ground these abstract semantic descriptions in reality—in the actual clicks and purchases that users make?
281.wh: Large language models are trained on general text, not on e-commerce behavior. An LLM might understand that a yoga mat is relaxing and eco-friendly, but it has no idea whether users who buy yoga mats also buy water bottles or fancy soaps. Meanwhile, learning item representations purely from user behavior (collaborative filtering) is blind to the item's actual properties—the system sees "people click this" but not *why*. Bridging these two views is crucial.
281.ap: The authors propose GenAIR, which starts by having an LLM infer an archetype for each item—the idealized profile of someone who would use this product. A yoga mat's archetype might be "health-conscious, environmentally aware, interested in fitness." The LLM generates this once and extracts its embedding. Then the system adds a behavioral calibration objective: it adjusts the embedding space so that items recommended together in reality (based on user interactions) are actually *close* in the embedding, grounding abstract archetypes in observed behavior.
281.ww: The archetype captures the semantic essence of an item (who it's for), and behavioral calibration ensures that essence aligns with real-world patterns. If an LLM imagines a yoga mat appeals to fitness enthusiasts but users pair it with meditation cushions, the calibration adjusts the embedding to reflect that pairing. This way, the system learns item relationships that are both semantically meaningful and empirically grounded.
281.po: GenAIR enables sequential recommendation systems to incorporate rich semantic understanding (from LLMs) while remaining grounded in what users actually do. The paper shows this improves recommendation quality, and the framework integrates seamlessly with existing models without major architecture changes—making it practical for real systems.

282.bp: Large language models can hallucinate—confidently making up facts. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) tries to fix this by having the model read from a document database before answering, so it at least has *something* true to work with. But if an attacker poisons those documents, they can trick the model into confidently repeating lies. As AI agents become central to business decisions, defending against poisoned knowledge is critical.
282.wh: RAG systems trust their document sources implicitly. If a document is in the database, it gets returned and fed to the model. An attacker who sneaks malicious documents into the database (by compromising sources, buying ad space, or other means) can manipulate the model's output without the model ever knowing. Traditional security assumes the source is trustworthy; that assumption breaks in open, adversarial environments.
282.ap: The authors propose SecureCollaRAG, which adds a validation layer: before using documents, the system checks their credibility using a graph neural network. Different documents point to each other and to external sources, and the GNN learns to score credibility by analyzing this network of references. Documents from consistent, well-attested sources score high; isolated, contradictory documents score low. Agents use only high-credibility documents, and the system flags low-credibility ones.
282.ww: This works because manipulation is hard at scale. An attacker can write one convincing lie, but getting *other* sources to corroborate it is expensive. The GNN-based credibility scoring captures this: legitimate knowledge appears in multiple, interconnected sources; misinformation tends to be isolated. By weighting documents based on this network analysis, the system is robust even if some sources are compromised.
282.po: Testing shows SecureCollaRAG resists poisoning attacks while preserving access to legitimate domain knowledge. The system maintains both robustness (rejecting malicious documents) and utility (accepting real knowledge) even when data is distributed unevenly across sources. This makes RAG systems safer for high-stakes applications like medical or legal AI agents.

283.bp: Generative AI systems like image generators and video models are trained on specific data, and they often fail when deployed in the real world where conditions differ. A model trained on stock photos might struggle with user-generated content. A model trained on English text might hallucinate when asked about emerging topics. Adapting these models to new environments without retraining from scratch is a critical practical problem.
283.wh: Models learn the patterns in their training data deeply. When you deploy them on data that looks different—different artistic style, new language, novel concepts—they often fail badly because the patterns have shifted. Retraining from scratch is expensive and slow. Meanwhile, simple fine-tuning can overfit to the new data and forget general knowledge. Balancing adaptation and retention is fundamentally tricky.
283.ap: The tutorial covers two complementary approaches. First, generalizable post-training techniques: methods that adapt a trained model to new conditions without catastrophic forgetting. Second, unified frameworks that handle both understanding (like image captioning) and generation (like image creation) together, since these tasks share knowledge. The tutorial walks through architectural designs for multi-modal models and mechanisms for handling distribution shifts.
283.ww: Post-training adaptation works because fine-tuning carefully is different from fine-tuning naively. Techniques like low-rank updates or prompt-based learning let the model stay faithful to general knowledge while learning new patterns. Unified understanding-and-generation frameworks work because captioning images teaches you what images should look like, and generating images teaches you what captions should describe—they're dual problems that reinforce each other.
283.po: The tutorial synthesizes research on out-of-distribution generalization for multi-modal models, giving practitioners concrete recipes for adapting models to new domains (different artistic styles, emerging concepts, new languages) without rebuilding from scratch. This is essential for deploying generative AI in the messy real world.

284.bp: Modern recommendation systems don't solve one problem—they solve many at once. They predict ratings, predict clicks, predict how long you'll watch, and all from the same data. These tasks compete: optimizing for clicks might hurt ratings, and vice versa. The art is figuring out which models should focus on which task and when to share knowledge between them. This paper proposes a system that adapts this sharing dynamically.
284.wh: Simple multi-task learning trains one shared model that tries to do everything. But different tasks need different features: predicting whether you'll *notice* an item requires different knowledge than predicting whether you'll *like* it if you do notice. Additionally, tasks have different importance—some matter more to the business or user than others, and that importance changes over time. A rigid architecture can't adapt to this shifting landscape.
284.ap: The authors propose Dynamic Experts Synergy: multiple expert models, each specializing in different knowledge, and a gating network that learns which experts to use for which task. The key innovation is identifying leader experts (heavily used by a task) and auxiliary experts (rarely used but containing complementary knowledge). The system then extracts knowledge from auxiliary experts in three ways: looking at their utility (do they help performance?), their diversity (do they cover different knowledge?), and task-relatedness (are they tuned to this task?).
284.ww: This works because it respects two truths about multi-task learning. First, not all knowledge is equally useful for all tasks—specialization matters. Second, even knowledge not directly used (low gating score) can still be valuable if you know how to translate it. By dynamically identifying which knowledge is leader (task-specific) and which is auxiliary (cross-cutting), the system avoids the rigidity of fixed architectures.
284.po: On five datasets, Dynamic Experts Synergy outperforms systems that either fully share knowledge or keep tasks completely separate. The framework adapts which expert contributes what, task-by-task, achieving better multi-task performance by treating auxiliary knowledge as a resource to be explicitly managed.
